title: Simple-root limit retractions and reflection-invariant kernels
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Groups are affine $F$-group schemes of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Write $\mathbf G_a,\mathbf G_m$ for [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected and $T\subseteq G$ a split maximal torus, that is, a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ and maximal among such subgroups. Write $N_G(T)$ for the subgroup functor normalizing $T$ after every scalar extension. Put $X=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and $Y=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf G_m,T)$, paired by $\chi\circ\eta(t)=t^{\langle\chi,\eta\rangle}$. Let $D\subset X\setminus\{0\}$ be finite, nonempty and $\mathbf Z$-linearly independent. For each $\alpha\in D$ let $J_\alpha\subseteq G$ be split reductive with maximal torus $T$ and roots exactly $\pm\alpha$, with conventions as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Denote its root groups by $U_\alpha,V_\alpha=U_{-\alpha}$ [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Assume $G$ is the smallest closed subgroup containing these $J_\alpha$, and that $V_\alpha$ commutes scheme-theoretically with $U_\beta$ whenever $\alpha\ne\beta$. Let $U,V$ be the smallest closed subgroups containing the $U_\alpha$, respectively the $V_\alpha$. For a cocharacter $\eta$, let $U_G(\eta)$ be the subgroup functor of points $g$ for which $\eta(t)g\eta(t)^{-1}$ extends to $t=0$ with value $1$, and let $Z_G(\eta)$ be the subgroup functor centralizing $\eta(\mathbf G_m)$ after every scalar extension. Assume $U,V$ are smooth and connected, $U=U_G(\lambda)$, $V=U_G(-\lambda)$, $Z_G(\lambda)=T$ for a $\lambda$ positive on $D$, and multiplication $V\times T\times U\to G$ is an open immersion. For every $\eta\in Y$ nonnegative on $D$, the action $(t,u)\mapsto\eta(t)u\eta(t)^{-1}$ extends to an action of the multiplicative monoid $\mathbf A^1$ on $U$. For each $\alpha\in D$ choose $\eta_\alpha\in Y$ with $\langle\alpha,\eta_\alpha\rangle=0$ and $\langle\beta,\eta_\alpha\rangle=m_\alpha>0$ for all $\beta\ne\alpha$. Evaluation at zero defines a group-scheme retraction $p_\alpha:U\to U_\alpha$. Its kernel $K_\alpha$ is smooth connected, multiplication gives $U_\alpha\ltimes K_\alpha\simeq U$, and $C_U(\eta_\alpha)=U_\alpha$. Any representative $n_\alpha\in N_{J_\alpha}(T)(F)$ of the rank-one nontrivial Weyl element satisfies $n_\alpha K_\alpha n_\alpha^{-1}=K_\alpha$. Centralizers and the assertions about kernels are assertions on all test algebras. No reductivity hypothesis is imposed on $G$.

source.place: Theorem 23.31, p.494; cocharacter limit homomorphisms in 13.28--13.33, pp.264--266. Supporting assertion: simple-root limit retractions and invariant kernels (Steinberg 1999, 5.11--5.13).

proof.text: First prove the asserted monoid extension, rather than assuming it. Fix $\eta$ nonnegative on $D$. Since $T$ commutes with $\lambda$, conjugation by $T$ preserves $U=U_G(\lambda)$ and $V=U_G(-\lambda)$, directly from their functor definitions. For each $\beta\in D$, the root formula is $\eta(t)u_\beta(a)\eta(t)^{-1}=u_\beta(t^{\langle\beta,\eta\rangle}a)$, so $U_\beta\subseteq P_\eta$, the closed limit-exists group supplied by the cocharacter structure theorem. The closed subgroup $U\cap P_\eta$ contains all the generators of $U$, hence equals $U$. Apply the functor description to the universal point over $F[U]$: its orbit extends over $F[U][t]$. This gives a morphism $\mathbf A^1\times U\to G$ which factors through $U$, since its restriction after inverting $t$ does and $F[U][t]\to F[U][t,t^{-1}]$ is injective. The same injectivity, also in two variables, extends the unit, monoid-action and group-homomorphism identities from invertible parameters to all parameters. Thus it is the required multiplicative-monoid action by group endomorphisms.

source.place: Root formula (135), p.431; Definition 13.21 and Proposition 13.24, pp.261--262; Propositions 13.28--13.29 and Theorem 13.33(a), pp.264--266.

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in D$ and the chosen $\eta_\alpha$, and write $p(u)=0\cdot u$ for the endomorphism from step 1. Such a choice is possible: the perfect pairing for the split torus and independence of $D$ give a rational cocharacter taking value $0$ on $\alpha$ and $1$ on the other elements; clearing denominators gives a common positive $m_\alpha$. If $D=\{\alpha\}$, take $\eta_\alpha=0$ and any $m_\alpha>0$. The root formula gives $p|_{U_\alpha}=\mathrm{id}$ and $p|_{U_\beta}=1$ for $\beta\ne\alpha$. Consequently the closed subgroup $p^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ of $U$ contains every generating root subgroup and is all of $U$. The morphism $p$ therefore factors through $U_\alpha$, and its restriction to that subgroup is the identity: this is the claimed group-scheme retraction.

source.place: Root formula (135), p.431; perfect character--cocharacter pairing in the root datum, Chapter 21 and Appendix C; limit homomorphism in Proposition 13.29, p.264.

proof.text: The monoid identity $s\cdot(0\cdot u)=0\cdot u$ shows that $p(u)$ is fixed under $\eta_\alpha$. Conversely an element fixed under $\eta_\alpha$ after every scalar extension has constant orbit on $\mathbf G_m$; uniqueness of its polynomial extension gives $p(u)=u$. Thus $C_U(\eta_\alpha)=\operatorname{im}(p)=U_\alpha$ as functors. Define $K=\ker(p)$, a closed normal subgroup of $U$. Multiplication $(a,k)\mapsto ak$ has inverse $u\mapsto(p(u),p(u)^{-1}u)$ on every test algebra, hence is an isomorphism of schemes $U_\alpha\times K\simeq U$. Its transported group law is $(a,k)(b,l)=(ab,b^{-1}kb\,l)$, which is exactly the conjugation semidirect product with normal factor $K$.

source.place: Proposition 13.29 and the limit-homomorphism calculation in Theorem 13.33(b), pp.264--266; explicit inverse and fixed-point calculation.

proof.text: Put $\eta=\eta_\alpha$ and $H=U_G(\eta)$. The cocharacter theorem makes $H$ smooth connected and gives its tangent space as the sum of the strictly positive $\eta$-weight spaces in $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. We check $\operatorname{Lie}(H)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(U)$. Step 1 gives $U\subseteq P_\eta$. On each $V_\beta$ the conjugation exponent for $-\eta$ is $\langle\beta,\eta\rangle\ge0$; closedness of $P_{-\eta}$ and generation therefore give $V\subseteq P_{-\eta}$. The Lie formulas imply that $\eta$ has only nonnegative weights on $\operatorname{Lie}(U)$, only nonpositive weights on $\operatorname{Lie}(V)$, and weight zero on $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. The same formulas for $\lambda$ and the assumed equalities $U=U_G(\lambda)$, $V=U_G(-\lambda)$, $Z_G(\lambda)=T$ give the $T$-stable direct sum $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(V)\oplus\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\operatorname{Lie}(U)$. Decompose the torus representation by applying the multiplicative-group weight-basis theorem successively to the factors of $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$; commuting factors preserve the preceding weight spaces. Every strictly positive $\eta$-weight of $\mathfrak g$ is therefore in $\operatorname{Lie}(U)$.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(c), pp.265--266, and the root conjugation formula (135), p.431; split-torus weight decomposition, Chapter 12.

proof.text: Upgrade the preceding tangent inclusion using positive-ray subgroups, so no assertion that arbitrary Lie inclusions imply subgroup inclusions is needed. Both $H$ and $U$ are smooth connected closed subgroups stable under conjugation by $T$ (the cocharacters commute with $T$). For each positive rational ray $R$ meeting the finite set of $T$-weights in $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$, let $V_R$ be the sum of all weight spaces of $\mathfrak g$ on that ray. Positivity on $\eta$ is constant along $R$, so the cocharacter Lie formula gives $V_R\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(H)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(U)$. The positive-ray subgroup theorem gives a smooth connected $T$-stable subgroup $S_R\subseteq G$ with tangent space $V_R$; its containment clause puts $S_R$ in both $H$ and $U$. These finitely many tangent spaces span $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$. Apply smooth-subgroup tangent generation in the ambient group $H$ to the closed subgroup $H\cap U$ containing all $S_R$. It follows that $H\cap U=H$, or $H\subseteq U$, as subgroup schemes. If there are no such rays, use the empty-family case of tangent generation.

source.place: Proposition 16.64(a), pp.348--349; Corollary 10.17, p.191; Theorem 13.33(c), pp.265--266.

proof.text: For $u\in U(A)$, the defining condition $p(u)=1$ is exactly that its $\eta$-conjugation orbit extends to zero with value $1$. Thus $K=U\cap U_G(\eta)$ on every commutative test algebra. Step 5 gives $U_G(\eta)\subseteq U$, so $K=U_G(\eta)=H$. Smoothness and connectedness of $K$ now follow from the cocharacter theorem. In particular this proves smoothness of the actual scheme-theoretic kernel, including infinitesimal test points, rather than merely its reduced subgroup.

source.place: Definition of the contraction kernel, Proposition 13.29, p.264; Theorem 13.33(a),(e), pp.265--266.

proof.text: Apply the Weyl-reflection realization and rank-one reflection statements to the reductive group $J_\alpha$, not to $G$. Since its only roots are $\pm\alpha$, its Weyl group has two elements, and every representative $n_\alpha$ of the nonidentity element acts on $X$ by $s_\alpha(\chi)=\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$. Preservation of the perfect pairing gives, for every $\chi\in X$, $\langle\chi,n_\alpha\eta_\alpha n_\alpha^{-1}\rangle=\langle s_\alpha^{-1}\chi,\eta_\alpha\rangle=\langle\chi,\eta_\alpha\rangle$, because $\langle\alpha,\eta_\alpha\rangle=0$. Hence $n_\alpha\eta_\alpha n_\alpha^{-1}=\eta_\alpha$ as cocharacters. On every test algebra, conjugation by $n_\alpha$ therefore takes an orbit extending with value $1$ to another such orbit; the same holds for $n_\alpha^{-1}$. Using $K=U_G(\eta_\alpha)$ from step 6 gives $n_\alpha K n_\alpha^{-1}=K$. All uses of reductive structure in this step concern the given $J_\alpha$.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(d),(e), pp.428--430; Theorem 21.37 and Corollary 21.38, pp.435--436; functor definition in Proposition 13.29, p.264.
